lead: A thread is the unit of CPU use inside a process. It has its own program counter, registers and stack, but shares the process's code, data and open files. Threads exist because creating a process is heavy, and because phones and servers have several cores. A music app can keep the screen alive while decoding a song; a web server can handle many requests in one process. This chapter shows what threads share, how user and kernel threads differ, the multithreading models, and why more threads do not always mean more speed.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for the process and its PCB.

sections.h3: What a thread owns and shares

blocks.text: A process is a program in execution. A thread is the smallest unit inside that process which the CPU can schedule. Each thread keeps a thread id, a program counter, a register set and a stack. The program counter holds the address of the next instruction. The register set holds values such as loop counters and function arguments. The stack holds local variables and return addresses. These items are private because two threads may be at different points in the same code.

Everything else belongs to the process. Code, global data, the heap, open files and signal handlers are shared. A file opened by one thread can be read by another. A global variable changed by one thread is seen by another, so Unit 3 must handle locking.

items: Responsiveness: one thread can keep the interface alive while another waits for a slow disk or network.
Resource sharing: threads use the same code, data and files without extra shared-memory setup.
Economy: creating a thread and switching between threads costs less than doing the same for processes.
Scalability: threads can use several cores at once, if the OS supports kernel-level threads.

rows: Shared address space inside the process

blocks.text: A process has its own address space; threads share one. Creating a thread is cheaper because no new address space is built. Threads communicate through shared variables; processes need shared memory or messages, as in Chapter 2.4. A bad write by one thread can crash the whole process.

sections.h3: User threads, kernel threads and three models

blocks.text: A user-level thread is created and managed by a library in user space. The kernel sees only the process. A kernel-level thread is created and managed by the OS, and the kernel schedules it directly.

items: Many-to-one: many user threads map to one kernel thread. Switching is fast because no kernel call is needed. If one thread makes a blocking system call, the kernel blocks the whole process, so all threads stall. All threads run on one kernel thread, so there is no true parallelism on multiple cores.

One-to-one: each user thread maps to one kernel thread. Linux and Windows use this. It gives true parallelism, and one blocking call blocks only its thread. Creating many threads costs kernel resources.

Many-to-many: m user threads map to n kernel threads, with m ≥ n. The library multiplexes threads. It avoids both limits but is complex. The two-level model also allows binding a chosen user thread to a kernel thread.

blocks.text: The model decides whether a blocking call stalls one thread or all threads, and whether two threads can run at the same instant on two cores.

Concurrency means several threads make progress over the same period, even by time slicing on one core. Parallelism means two threads execute at the same instant on two cores. Two threads on one core are concurrent, not parallel. Data parallelism divides the same operation over different data: four threads each filter a quarter of an image. Task parallelism gives different tasks to different threads: one thread decodes audio, another draws the screen.

blocks.where: S(N) is the speedup with N cores; s is the serial fraction, with 0 ≤ s ≤ 1; N is the number of cores. As N → ∞, S → 1 ÷ s.

blocks.text: A thread library gives calls to create and join threads. Common libraries are POSIX pthreads, Windows threads and Java threads. Which thread the scheduler picks is Chapter 2.8. More threads than cores does not increase speed.

examples.question: An image-filter app spends 20% of its single-core run time in code that cannot be parallelised. Find the speedup with 4 cores, and the best possible speedup with any number of cores.
steps: The serial fraction is s = 20% = 0.20. The parallel fraction is 1 − s = 0.80.
For N = 4 cores, use S(N) = 1 ÷ (s + (1 − s) ÷ N).
S(4) = 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5. The app runs at most 2.5 times faster on 4 cores.
As N → ∞, (1 − s) ÷ N → 0, so S → 1 ÷ s = 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5. The best possible speedup is 5 times.
examples.answer: The 4-core speedup is 2.5 times, and the best possible speedup with any number of cores is 5 times.
examples.check:
s = 0.20
N = 4
speedup_4 = 1 / (s + (1 - s) / N)
speedup_inf = 1 / s
print(speedup_4)
print(speedup_inf)

traps: A thread does not have its own address space. Threads in one process share code, data, heap and open files; only registers, program counter, stack and thread id are private.
Two threads on one core are concurrent by time slicing, not parallel. Parallelism needs at least two cores at the same instant.
In many-to-one, one blocking system call stalls every thread in the process, and there is no true parallelism.
User-level threads are invisible to the kernel; kernel-level threads are scheduled by the kernel. Do not say the kernel schedules user threads directly in many-to-one.
Amdahl's law caps speedup at 1 ÷ s, where s is the serial fraction. More cores cannot remove serial work.

quiz.q: Define a thread and list four items private to it.
quiz.a: A thread is the smallest schedulable unit inside a process. Private items: thread id, program counter, register set and stack.

quiz.q: Why can threads in one process share an open file but not a stack?
quiz.a: Open files belong to the process. Each thread has its own call path and local variables, so it needs its own stack.

quiz.q: A task is 25% serial. Find its speedup on 4 cores.
Why does the many-to-one model give no true parallelism?
quiz.a: All user threads map to one kernel thread. The kernel can schedule that one thread on only one core at a time, so only one thread executes at an instant.
Many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many. The two-level model is a variant of many-to-many.
Concurrency means threads make progress over the same period, possibly by time slicing. Parallelism means threads execute at the same instant on separate cores.

quiz.q: Which model does Linux use, and what is one cost?
quiz.a: Linux uses one-to-one. Each user thread needs a kernel thread, so creating many threads costs kernel resources.

quiz.q: A program has s = 0.10. Can 16 cores give 10× speedup? Explain.
quiz.a: No. S(16) = 1 ÷ (0.10 + 0.90 ÷ 16) = 1 ÷ 0.15625 = 6.4 times. The serial 10% caps speedup at 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10 times, and 16 cores reach only 6.4 times.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, thread pools, async runtimes and server event loops manage thousands of tasks without one OS thread per task. Languages add green threads, goroutines or virtual threads, which the runtime maps onto a smaller set of kernel threads. Profilers show that lock contention and false sharing can erase multicore gains. Search for goroutines, Java virtual threads, thread pools and Amdahl's law calculators.
